paper.title: LOBO - Evaluation of Generalization Deficiencies in Twitter Bot Classifiers
paper.venue: Proceedings of the 2018 Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC 2018)
paper.version: arXiv:1809.09684v1, 2018-09-25; PDF states published at ACSAC 2018
paper.page_convention: 1-based PDF page numbers; equal to printed page numbers in this file

text_evidence_sources: direct inspection of all 12 selected visual crops

claims.claim: High conventional account-level accuracy does not imply generalization to an unseen bot family.

evidence.note: LightGBM reaches 97.84% on C30K and 93.93% on C500 under conventional random splitting.
C500 full-model mean is 94.29%, while held-family LOBO mean is 57.51%.

caveats: The result is limited to the collected Twitter classes and acquisition protocols.
Held-family target accuracy is bot-only recall and does not measure deployment false positives.

claims.claim: LOBO performance is highly family-dependent even after balancing each included family to 500 accounts.

evidence.note: Per-family LOBO accuracy ranges from 0.71% for F to 98.14% for B.

caveats: Table 6 contains 13 target rows although the text says 14, and U is undefined in Table 1.

claims.claim: A small number of labeled target-family examples can rapidly recover performance for some, but not all, families.

evidence.note: Mean accuracy rises with target samples, while selected families show sharply different curves.
A and F improve rapidly; H remains 81.6% at 256 samples and V/T/W improve little.

caveats: Target test size shrinks as samples are moved into training.
The experiment uses one sampled C500 dataset and does not report full implementation settings.

claims.claim: The paper's t-SNE visualization is consistent with some families being feature-separable and others overlapping real users.

evidence.note: Star Wars and Bursty form visibly distinct strands, whereas Honeypot points overlap many real-user strands.

caveats: t-SNE settings and seed are not reported.
A two-dimensional embedding is qualitative evidence and cannot establish the classification mechanism.

claims.claim: LOBO results are mostly stable across C500 resampling, with notable exceptions.

evidence.note: The paper reports standard deviation below 4% for almost all targets, except A at 24% and E at 13%.

caveats: Per-repeat values and the full per-class uncertainty table are not published in the PDF.

claims.claim: Exact numerical reproduction is blocked by missing artifacts and internal reporting inconsistencies.

evidence.note: The paper states 30 dimensions, while Table 2 visibly enumerates 29 entries and includes User ID.
Headers, row semantics, and the reported 54.88% mean cannot be reconciled from displayed values.
U is undefined, X disappears, and 13 displayed C500 targets conflict with the stated 14 classes.

caveats: A released code/data snapshot could resolve some ambiguities, but none is identified in the PDF.

claims.claim: Account bot classification is not a valid substitute for community authenticity assessment.

evidence.note: The complete pipeline represents and labels individual accounts as bot or user; no community construct is defined.
Features are account profile and tweet aggregates, not group coordination, provenance, common control, or deceptive intent.

caveats: Bot scores may be useful as one account-level signal inside a broader community evidence model.

claims.claim: For CogGuard, LOBO should be transferred as leave-campaign, leave-platform, and forward-time evaluation with group-level leakage controls.

evidence.note: LOBO supplies the general group-held-out principle: remove the complete target domain from training before evaluation.
The large random-split versus held-group gap motivates analogous external-domain tests.

caveats: The campaign/platform/time extension is a report inference and is not evaluated in the source paper.
